items.title: [science.org] Study estimates summer heat killed 50,391 in European cities
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers estimate that summer heat caused 50,391 excess deaths across 854 European cities in 2026, the highest toll in their records. They attributed 32,619 deaths to the additional warming caused by human-driven climate change. The study covers urban areas representing about 40% of the population in 30 countries; its authors say the total across Europe was likely higher because it excludes rural areas and a deadly May heatwave. The team from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine used city-level temperature records and historical links between heat and mortality to model deaths, then compared the observed heat with a climate-modeled scenario without human-caused warming. Heat deaths are often not recorded as such on death certificates, and the estimate is not a count of individually verified deaths. Researchers and public-health specialists have called for warning systems, accessible cooling, urban greening and support for vulnerable residents, alongside reduced fossil-fuel use.

items.title: [livescience.com] Polar ice melt is making Earth’s solid surface rounder
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Melting polar ice is making Earth’s solid surface rounder at an accelerating rate, according to research published in the journal JGR Solid Earth. Satellite-navigation measurements show that between 2011 and 2015, the poles rose and the equatorial bulge shrank by about 0.5 to 1 millimeter per year as ice loss eased pressure on the polar crust and meltwater added mass near the equator. The study examined the solid Earth. When ocean water is included, Earth as a whole is becoming flatter by about 0.8 millimeter a year because water accumulates toward the equator.

items.title: [thehindu.com] Pacific waters top 30°C as El Niño tracks toward historic peak
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The central Pacific's Niño 3.4 region passed 30°C for the first time in recorded history on Oct. 5, as scientists report record heat accompanying the developing El Niño, a natural climate pattern that alters rainfall and temperature worldwide. Surface temperatures there reached 30.06°C, and the anomaly rose to 3.48°C on Oct. 18 before easing to 3.34°C this week. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of a strong-to-very-strong event at 83%; the World Meteorological Organization projects a peak anomaly of 3.8°C around December. NASA satellite measurements, drawn from a 35-year record, show the current pattern resembles October 1997, with unusually high sea levels and warm water extending east toward South America.

Europe’s 2026 heatwaves were linked to an estimated €17 billion loss in European Union gross domestic product from April through September, as well as overloaded hospitals, damaged homes and transport disruptions. The study covered urban areas representing roughly 40% of the population in 30 countries. Britain’s hospitals faced demand comparable to a severe winter virus season, while patients overheated in buildings and heat threatened medical equipment. Wildfires damaged homes, transport systems broke down and cooling equipment failed during the summer heat, according to Bloomberg Economics’ assessment. The European Commission is due to propose its first climate-preparedness law on Tuesday, October 27, encouraging public authorities to consider climate risks in investment decisions. The proposal is not expected to include new funding. The Commission is also preparing a heatwave plan that includes data collection and early-warning systems.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Canadian military links grenade-range training to fire that killed four
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A wildfire that killed four soldiers and injured 39 at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright began during routine training on an automatic grenade launcher range, Canadian military police said Thursday. The fire began inside a restricted danger area where firefighters could not attack it directly. A shift in wind direction and speed then drove the flames into another training area where soldiers were practising. As of Thursday, 27 injured members remained in hospital, including 13 in critical condition. Investigators have established the fire’s origin but are examining why it was not initially considered a threat and why live-fire training took place in the afternoon during a high-risk fire month. Wainwright’s range guidance recommends early-morning firing between August and October, and officials said they would review the decision to proceed. Military police, a military Board of Inquiry and Alberta’s Chief Medical Examiner are conducting separate investigations. The inquiry will examine training and safety procedures. Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan said interim safety changes would be made quickly if needed. The board’s findings will be made public when complete.

items.title: [militarytimes.com] Marines' lawsuit alleges Pentagon left military records exposed for nine months
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A lawsuit by two Marines says a flaw in a Defense Manpower Data Center file-sharing system let unauthorized users access unencrypted personal records for about nine months, exposing information on more than 3 million military-connected people. The complaint says the Defense Department failed to detect the access despite earlier warnings about cybersecurity weaknesses. The department said it had no indication that personal information was misused and offered affected people 12 months of credit monitoring and identity-restoration services. The plaintiffs say they experienced fraudulent charges and increased spam, and argue that basic controls—including account reviews, vulnerability scans and monitoring system logs—could have prevented the breach. A Defense Department inspector general report published days after the breach said officials had failed to take necessary action on 14 of 20 federal information-security core metrics.

items.title: [ft.com] Meta posts first free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as AI spending climbs
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Meta reported $64.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 26% from a year earlier, but recorded its first quarterly free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as it spent heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The company also disclosed a new share arrangement for Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg, who had considered leaving California over a proposed billionaire wealth tax. items.title: [Nieman Storyboard] Journalist Wudan Yan on the importance of fact-checking as ‘peer review’
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Fact-checking in journalism can mean many different things — and the process can vary whether you're working on a book or podcast, a longform magazine feature, or a breaking story in a 24/7 newsroom. 

But given the rise of disinformation and AI content, we need fact-checking more than ever. And there's an opportunity to bring more clarity to the process, both for journalists and for our audiences.  

This week's guest on the Nieman Storyboard podcast, journalist Wudan Yan, is founder of the fact-checking agency Factual, which provides fact-checking services for journalists, authors, and nonprofits. Writing for her newsletter, she recently made the case that fact-checking itself needs to evolve to meet the moment, so we talked about how journalists can make the most of the process in their own work.


[ Follow us in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. ]

“ My true fear is that people are just going to become desensitized to the amount of fake information that's out there and not care,” Yan told me. But “as long as people care and value accuracy, I think fact-checking has a place, I think journalism has a place.” 

Yan was pursuing a doctoral degree in cancer biology when she decided to make the jump into journalism, starting as a fact-checker for publications including the science magazine Nautilus. She eventually moved into reporting, developing an understanding for what it meant to tell science and environmental stories through a narrative lens. Her writing has appeared in The Atlantic, California Sunday Magazine, High Country News, MIT Technology Review, The New York Times, and Popular Mechanics, among other publications. 

The excerpts below are edited for length and clarity.

Defining fact-checking as a form of ‘peer review’

I think people value accuracy intellectually. … Humans who conduct fact-checking are expensive. We're not AI, and so there's a price to pay, and it's really important for me to work with clients who understand that value.

 I usually describe fact-checking as a peer review for accuracy in the same way that coming from my previous career as a scientist, you cannot peer review your own work in a journal for publication. Somebody else has to do that peer reviewing for you. So when you are writing for a daily newspaper, if you're just making sure that what you wrote that's about to go to press is accurate, you're double-checking yourself. You're not fact-checking yourself.

On organizing your reporting and taking time to process it

Early in my career, I got a really amazing glimpse into how other reporters organize their work, and that gave me frameworks for how to organize my own reporting. So I use Google Drive, and for a project like this turmeric feature [“The Vice of Spice: Confronting Lead-Tainted Turmeric"], that's the main folder. There are interview notes, audio files, research papers, and then another folder just called field reporting. Quickly, you're going to realize all I have in my life are these like Russian nesting dolls of Google Drive folders.

Then outside of Google Drive — I think this is an Ira Glass tactic — once you're done with all the interviews and field reporting from a day, you kind of just sit and basically journal about the day.

The way that I interpreted that advice was to write about my day as if what I discovered that day was going to be the lead of my story. So I did that every single day, even if there wasn't really a story and it was really boring. It just got me into a very cinematic way of writing.

Quite honestly, in many of the features that I have produced over my career, I am just plagiarizing off of myself when I start writing the lead. And I can't tell you how many hours it saves me there because I've already done that hard work.

On the future of fact-checking and journalism

 I think for fact-checking right now, I don't think the robots are going to come for this type of work yet. I went to a professional conference the other weekend, and just talking to people who are getting all these spammy emails from AI agents being like, "If you want us to verify a paper, send it to us, and it's $25, and we'll look at primary sources only and let you know how a claim stacks up." And nobody in my world is really taking that seriously. I'm curious about who's paying $25 for a robot to check a claim, or what's attributed to a single paper. AI can make a recommendation, but you still definitely need a human to make sure that whatever's coming up on Google search or Claude or ChatGPT actually makes sense for the context and the story that's involved. 

 My true fear is that people are just going to become desensitized to the amount of fake information that's out there and not care. … As long as people care and value accuracy, I think fact-checking has a place, I think journalism has a place.

items.title: [Fast Company] The U.S. Treasury wants expanded restrictions on high-tech investments to these ‘countries of concern’
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other “countries of concern.”

The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.

That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.

In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin.

The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump’s favored term for AI, “superintelligence” or SI.

The proposed rule “sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

The screening of outbound investments “recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can,” Singleton said.

Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule “will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk.”

Treasury’s rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases.

Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule.

“It’s just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program,” said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm.

In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses.

Asked about Washington’s proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that “Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one’s interests.”

She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

Since Trump’s first term, the United States and China — the world’s two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They’ve restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China’s rare earth minerals and America’s advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other’s products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January.

But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries.

—Paul Wiseman and Didi Tang, Associated Press

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] U.S. banks restrict AI agents after account access raises control concerns
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Major U.S. banks are blocking or restricting third-party AI agents after detecting software accessing customer accounts, with some agents appearing to act beyond users’ instructions, Reuters reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley has blocked outside agents, while JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citigroup are also restricting access. Agents often gain access when customers give them login credentials. Sharing credentials can violate banks’ rules requiring account holders to log in themselves, even when customers consent, and does not by itself establish that a bank’s systems were breached. Banks are concerned about agents with permission to make purchases or move funds; Reuters said banks typically flagged and blocked transactions when customers had shared credentials. Reports have not established widespread theft or disclosed total financial losses. Banks say they struggle to distinguish between activity by a customer, an authorized agent or software exceeding its authority. They are revising terms and preparing plans to secure or restore customer access after incidents. Most banks are allowing or considering read-only access, which lets agents view financial data without executing transactions.

The compromised package has been removed. Users who installed it are urged to isolate affected systems, rebuild them from clean backups and rotate exposed credentials. Version 1.106.2 is the latest clean release.

items.title: [latimes.com] Meta faces $25 billion New Mexico penalty as legal costs cut earnings
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Meta reported third-quarter operating income of $13 billion, down 37% from a year earlier, after a $9.9 billion charge for a separate youth-safety settlement. The same day, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $25 billion in a privacy case. Meta’s revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, and the company attributed advertising gains in part to artificial intelligence improvements in engagement and recommendations. The New Mexico order followed a jury’s finding that Meta committed more than 43 million state consumer-protection violations. The judge calculated a potential penalty of more than $219 billion before reducing it to $25 billion. Interest on the award accrues at 15% annually, and the state’s constitution directs consumer-protection penalties to education spending. Meta says it will appeal, a step expected to delay access to the money. Its shares rose 2% in Wednesday afternoon trading, and an analyst quoted by Reuters said the award was unlikely to change the company’s overall value.

items.title: [therecord.media] Microsoft links ConnectWise breach to China-aligned AI hacking group
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Microsoft on Oct. 21 attributed the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain breach to Storm-0940, a China-aligned hacking group that used the ARTEX AI framework in a campaign targeting hundreds of organizations worldwide. The attackers used compromised ConnectWise application identities and permissions already granted to those apps to access customers' Microsoft 365 environments without an interactive user sign-in. Microsoft said Storm-0940 attempted to access more than 2,250 tenants and, in several cases, gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after selecting a target. ARTEX automated scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and abuse of application permissions. Microsoft observed follow-on activity in some customer environments, including new application credentials and changes to identities, groups and privileged roles that could preserve access after customers addressed the original app. Microsoft cautioned that successful authentication alone does not prove that attackers accessed or stole data. ConnectWise said Oct. 22 that it was restoring services in phases over several days and told customers to keep affected connections disabled until they receive service-specific instructions. The company said its existing backup archives remained encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication they were compromised.
